title: Follow the guarantee
hook: A blue card touches the scanner. What must the gate do?

challenge.stem: A machine follows three rules: if its temperature is below 5°C, its blue lamp is on; if it detects smoke, its red lamp is on; if its battery is low, its amber lamp is on. Its temperature is 3°C and its battery is not low. Nothing is said about smoke. Which statement must be true?
challenge.explanation: Three degrees is below five, so the temperature fact triggers the blue-lamp rule. No stated fact settles the other lamps.
challenge.proofPrompt: Draw an arrow for a rule you use. Which given fact belongs at its start?

distractorReasons.A: No information is given about smoke or any other reason for the red lamp to be on.
distractorReasons.C: The battery rule tells us what happens when the battery is low. With a charged battery, it leaves the amber lamp free to be on or off.
distractorReasons.D: The rule guarantees blue, but does not exclude red or amber.

reviewQuestion.stem: Every parcel with a triangle label is sealed. Every parcel with an oval label has a tracking tag. Parcel P has a triangle label and no oval label. Which statement must be true?

options.text: P is the only sealed parcel.

reviewQuestion.explanation: The triangle label triggers triangle → sealed. The other rule supplies no guarantee about parcels without oval labels.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Choose a label on the parcel. Show exactly what its rule promises.

distractorReasons.A: No oval label does not imply no tracking tag.
distractorReasons.B: The facts explicitly say P has no oval label.
distractorReasons.D: Nothing restricts how many other parcels are sealed.

title: Required or enough?
hook: Mia handed in her form. Has she made the final?
takeaway: A requirement is something you need. A guarantee is enough by itself.
steps: Name the result being discussed.
Separate requirements from guarantees.
Check what the facts actually establish.
pitfall: Meeting one requirement does not prove that every requirement is met.

challenge.stem: To use the science lab, you must finish the safety lesson. An invitation from the supervisor guarantees a turn in the lab. Mira finishes the safety lesson but has no invitation. What do the rules tell us about Mira’s turn?

options.text: Mira gets a turn only. Missing out is impossible.
Mira misses out only. Getting a turn is impossible.
Neither outcome fits. The two rules conflict.
Both outcomes fit. Mira could get a turn or miss out.

challenge.explanation: Mira meets the safety requirement. The invitation is one guaranteed route. The rules allow another way to get a turn, and also allow Mira to miss out.
challenge.proofPrompt: For each outcome you think fits, check it against both rules.

distractorReasons.A: Finishing the lesson is required. The rule never promises a turn for doing it.
distractorReasons.B: Other routes may exist, so missing the invitation cannot rule out a turn.
distractorReasons.C: Mira can finish the lesson without an invitation. Both rules still hold.

reviewQuestion.stem: To be displayed at an exhibition, a painting must be dry. A curator’s gold sticker guarantees that a painting is displayed. Which description correctly distinguishes the two conditions?

options.text: Being dry is necessary for display; a gold sticker is sufficient for display.
Being dry is sufficient for display; a gold sticker is necessary for display.
Both being dry and having a gold sticker are necessary for display.
Both being dry and having a gold sticker are sufficient for display.

reviewQuestion.explanation: Display → dry makes dryness necessary. Gold sticker → display makes the sticker sufficient. A displayed painting need not have a sticker, and a dry painting need not be displayed.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Draw the arrow for each condition. What does each arrow tell you?

distractorReasons.B: This reverses both stated relationships.
distractorReasons.C: The sticker guarantees display, but is not stated to be required for every display.
distractorReasons.D: Dryness is required, but dryness alone is not stated to guarantee display.

visualDirection: Show an induction card as one required gate and an invitation as a guaranteed route. Two legal outcome cards keep access unresolved when only induction is known.

challenge.stem: At an event, everyone follows these rules: only registered volunteers carry radios; anyone carrying a radio wears an ID badge; a visitor may enter the control room only if carrying a radio. Tali is a visitor who has entered the control room. Which conclusion must follow?

options.text: Every registered volunteer has entered the control room.
Tali is registered and wears an ID badge.
Everyone with an ID badge carries a radio.
Tali is the only registered visitor.

challenge.explanation: Control-room entry → radio → registered volunteer, and radio → ID badge. Tali’s entry triggers both requirements. No rule limits the number of visitors.
challenge.proofPrompt: Rewrite all three rules as arrows and trace Tali’s entry to each required fact.

distractorReasons.A: Registration is a requirement of radio carrying, not a guarantee of room entry.
distractorReasons.C: This reverses radio → ID badge.

reviewQuestion.stem: A library display case cannot be opened without a key. The key can be collected only if a librarian signs a form on the day it is collected. No librarian has signed a form today. Everyone follows these rules, and a key must be collected today before it is used. What must be true today?

options.text: The display case must be empty.
Every signed form would guarantee an open case.
The display case cannot be opened.
A key was collected despite the missing signature.

reviewQuestion.explanation: No librarian signed a form today, so no key can be collected today. Since today’s opening requires a key collected today, opening is blocked too.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Put each rule into your own words. Which cases fit what happened today?

distractorReasons.A: The rules say nothing about the case’s contents.
distractorReasons.B: A signature is required for key collection, but does not force collection or opening.
distractorReasons.D: Key collection requires the signature that is absent.

hook: You hear no beep. Can you rule out a valid scan?

challenge.stem: During each test, if a valid token is scanned, the green light flashes. If the green light flashes, a log entry is saved. Test 12 produced no log entry. Which statement must be true about Test 12?

options.text: No token of any kind was scanned.

challenge.explanation: Valid scan → green flash → log entry. No log entry implies no green flash, which implies no valid scan. A failed scan, no scan, and other details remain unspecified.
challenge.proofPrompt: Start with Test 12. How far can you work back along the rules?

distractorReasons.B: The rules do not exclude an invalid token being scanned.
distractorReasons.C: An invalid scan is possible but not forced; there may have been no scan.
distractorReasons.D: No rule connects power to log entries.

challenge.stem: If a parcel is fragile, it receives a red sticker. If a parcel needs urgent delivery, it also receives a red sticker. Parcel R is not fragile. Owen says, “R cannot have a red sticker.” Which case best disproves Owen’s claim while obeying both rules?

options.text: R is fragile and has a red sticker.
R is fragile and has no red sticker.
R is urgent, not fragile, and has a red sticker.
R is not urgent, not fragile, and has no red sticker.

challenge.explanation: An urgent, non-fragile parcel must receive a red sticker under the second rule. This satisfies the stated fact and both rules, but makes Owen’s claim false.
challenge.proofPrompt: Check your case against the parcel facts, both rules and Owen’s claim.

distractorReasons.A: It contradicts the given fact that R is not fragile.
distractorReasons.B: It contradicts both the given fact and fragile → red sticker.
distractorReasons.D: This agrees with Owen’s conclusion, so it is not a counterexample.

Devon is a marshal outside the club and has no blue cap.

reviewQuestion.explanation: A marshal outside the club can have the cap while the claim “Devon is a club member” is false.

distractorReasons.A: This case fits the rules, but it cannot disprove membership because Devon is a member in this case.
distractorReasons.C: Both the given cap and the club’s rule require a blue cap.
distractorReasons.D: Marshals have blue caps, and we are told Devon has one.

title: Rewrite the exception
hook: The coach is away. Can you still collect the equipment?
takeaway: Read “Y unless X” as “if X does not happen, then Y”.
steps: Identify the exception or condition.
Rewrite the full sentence using if or if not.
Apply only the direction actually stated.
pitfall: “Unless” does not automatically mean “if and only if”; the exception happening may leave the result open.

challenge.stem: A fun run goes ahead unless there is a storm warning. A runner cannot start unless wearing a numbered bib. There is no storm warning, and Leo has no numbered bib. Everyone follows the rules. What must be true?

options.text: The whole fun run is cancelled because Leo has no bib.
The fun run goes ahead, but Leo cannot start.
Leo may start because there is no storm warning.
Every runner who has a bib must start.

challenge.explanation: No storm warning → fun run goes ahead. Starting → numbered bib, so no bib → Leo cannot start. These rules govern different results and must both be respected.
challenge.proofPrompt: Put each rule into your own words. Which fact starts each rule?

distractorReasons.A: The no-warning fact guarantees the event goes ahead; Leo’s missing bib restricts Leo.
distractorReasons.C: The weather rule does not remove the bib requirement.
distractorReasons.D: A bib is required to start, but does not force a runner to start.

challenge.stem: A rectangular sheet covers −4 ≤ x ≤ 4 and −3 ≤ y ≤ 3, with x right and y up. Fold the right half left across x = 0, then fold the upper half down across y = 0. Punch a tiny point through all layers at (−1, −2). After fully unfolding, which set gives all hole centres?

distractorReasons.B: This swaps the x and y distances rather than reflecting them.
distractorReasons.C: This undoes only the horizontal fold and misses the vertical reflection.

reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Show the positions after each fold opens. Count different positions.

distractorReasons.A: The punch has y=0, and a horizontal reflection keeps y=0; it cannot create y=±2.
distractorReasons.C: The vertical reflection still creates a second centre because x=−2 is away from x=0.
distractorReasons.D: This exchanges x and y instead of reflecting across the stated lines.

challenge.stem: Two taps fill an empty tank at constant independent rates of 6 litres/minute and 4 litres/minute. At the same time a drain removes 2 litres/minute. All three operate continuously until the tank contains 120 litres. How many minutes does this take?

challenge.stem: Eight teams are scheduled to play every other team exactly once. Three of those matches are cancelled and not replaced. Afterwards, the top two teams play one additional final. How many matches are actually played in total?
challenge.explanation: The original round-robin contains 8×7÷2=28 unordered pairs. Remove the three cancellations and add the extra final: 28−3+1=26.
challenge.proofPrompt: How did you count every match just once?

distractorReasons.A: 25 removes the cancelled matches but forgets the additional final.
distractorReasons.C: 54 begins with 8×7=56 and counts each original pairing twice.
distractorReasons.D: 29 includes the final but ignores all three cancellations.

reviewQuestion.stem: A straight 36 m fence needs a post at each end and every 4 m in between. The posts at the two ends are already installed, and no interior posts exist yet. How many more posts are needed?
reviewQuestion.explanation: There are 36÷4=9 gaps and therefore 10 post positions along the straight line. Two endpoint posts already exist, so 10−2=8 more posts are required.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: What does each mark in your fence sketch stand for?

distractorReasons.B: Seven results from treating nine gaps as nine posts and then subtracting two.
distractorReasons.C: Nine is the number of gaps, not the number of missing posts.
distractorReasons.D: Ten is the total post count, including the two already installed.

title: Check the interval boundary
hook: One pass works from ten until one. The next starts at one. Which pass works at half past twelve?
takeaway: A person can be inside only while their pass is valid.
steps: Mark the time you need.
Check who can enter or must leave at that time.
Check that the room has enough space.
pitfall: Counting expired groups, excluding a group at its valid start, or ignoring capacity.

challenge.stem: Visitors with the same pass can arrive separately. A pass works from its start time and everyone must be out by its end. Group A: 4 visitors, 09:00–11:00. B: 6 visitors, 10:00–12:00. C: 3 visitors, 11:00–13:00. D: 5 visitors, 11:30–14:00. The room holds at most 8 people. At exactly 11:00, what is the greatest number of these visitors who could be inside?
challenge.explanation: At 11:00, A has expired and D has not started. B and C are eligible, giving nine potential visitors. Capacity limits the actual maximum to eight, attainable with all six from B and two from C.
challenge.proofPrompt: Who could be there at that moment? Show how they fit.

distractorReasons.A: Nine is the eligible total, but it exceeds the room capacity of eight.
distractorReasons.B: Thirteen also includes group A, whose access ends exactly at 11:00.
distractorReasons.D: Six excludes group C even though access includes its 11:00 start.

reviewQuestion.stem: Access includes the start time and excludes the end; visitors may arrive whenever they choose within their window and must leave by its end. There is no room capacity limit. Group A has 4 visitors with access 11:00–14:00, B has 3 with access 12:00–15:00, and C has 6 with access 13:30–16:30. At exactly 14:00, what is the maximum possible number inside?
reviewQuestion.explanation: A must already be out at 14:00. B and C can both be present, so the maximum is 3+6=9. For example, all B and C visitors can arrive before 14:00 and remain inside then.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Which windows include the target time? Could those visitors be there together?

distractorReasons.B: Thirteen incorrectly includes A at its excluded end time.
distractorReasons.C: Three counts B but ignores C, whose window has already begun.
distractorReasons.D: Six counts C but ignores B, whose window is still valid.

title: Split the number blocks
hook: If a book uses 429 digits to number its pages, could you just divide by three?
takeaway: Find where the counting pattern changes or repeats.
steps: For pages, group numbers with the same digit length.

challenge.stem: A booklet numbers every page consecutively from 1, with no leading zeros and no omitted page numbers. Its printed page numbers use exactly 558 digits. What is the last page number?
challenge.explanation: Pages 1–9 use 9 digits and 10–99 use 90×2=180, for 189 through page 99. The remaining 558−189=369 digits make 123 three-digit pages. The last page is 99+123=222.
challenge.proofPrompt: How many digits belong to each group of pages?

distractorReasons.A: 186 is 558÷3, incorrectly assuming every page number uses three digits.
distractorReasons.B: 123 counts only the three-digit pages and omits the first 99 pages.
distractorReasons.C: 223 adds 100 instead of 99, producing an off-by-one error.

reviewQuestion.stem: Two bells ring together at 09:05. One then rings every 6 minutes and the other every 10 minutes, continuing at these exact intervals. What is their first simultaneous ring strictly after 09:50?
reviewQuestion.explanation: They coincide every LCM(6,10)=30 minutes. From 09:05, shared times are 09:35, 10:05, 10:35 and so on. The first strictly after 09:50 is 10:05.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Which ringing times meet both conditions?

distractorReasons.A: 09:35 is a shared time but occurs before the required 09:50 threshold.
distractorReasons.B: 09:55 is 50 minutes after the anchor, divisible by ten but not six.
distractorReasons.C: 10:35 is shared but not the first qualifying time; 10:05 occurs earlier.

challenge.stem: A club needs at least 23 badges. Badges are sold only in packs of 8 for $7 or packs of 12 for $10. Any number of either pack may be bought, mixing is allowed, and leftovers are allowed. What is the least possible total cost?
challenge.explanation: Two 12-packs provide 24 badges for $20. A mixed pair provides only 20 badges for $17, while three 8-packs cost $21. With no 12-packs, at least three 8-packs are needed; with exactly one 12-pack, at least two 8-packs are needed and cost $24. Two or more 12-packs cost at least $20.
challenge.proofPrompt: How can you rule out a cheaper purchase?

distractorReasons.B: $17 buys 8+12=20 badges, fewer than the required 23.
distractorReasons.C: $21 buys three 8-packs and is valid, but two 12-packs are cheaper.
distractorReasons.D: $24 buys two 8-packs plus a 12-pack; it is valid but costs more than $20.

hook: A card rule says every vowel has an even number on the back. Could a seven break the rule?

challenge.stem: A building rule says: anyone entering after 18:00 without an escort must wear a badge. Four records have missing details. A: entered at 19:00, no escort, badge unknown. B: entered at 19:00 with an escort, badge unknown. C: entered at 17:00, no escort, badge unknown. D: entered at 20:00, no badge, escort unknown. Which is the smallest set of missing details that covers every record where a violation of this rule could be hidden?
challenge.explanation: A breaks the rule if no badge was worn. D breaks it if there was no escort. B has an escort and C entered before 18:00, so neither satisfies the full condition. Check A’s badge and D’s escort.
challenge.proofPrompt: What would a broken rule look like in these records?

distractorReasons.A: D may also hide a violation: entering late without a badge is forbidden if D had no escort.
distractorReasons.B: B has an escort, so B cannot violate the no-escort condition regardless of the badge result; this option misses D.
distractorReasons.C: B and C cannot violate this particular rule on the stated facts, while the unresolved A and D cases remain unchecked.

reviewQuestion.stem: Each parcel record has its service type on one side and its weight on the other. Service is either express or standard. Four visible sides read EXPRESS, STANDARD, 1 kg, and 3 kg. To test the rule “Every express parcel weighs less than 2 kg” for these four records, what is the smallest set of records that must be turned over?
reviewQuestion.explanation: Turn EXPRESS to check whether its weight is at least 2 kg. Turn 3 kg to check whether its service is express. STANDARD is not constrained by this rule, and a 1 kg parcel cannot violate it whatever its service type.
reviewQuestion.proofPrompt: Which hidden sides could show that the rule is broken?

distractorReasons.A: The 1 kg record already satisfies the weight requirement if it is express; this misses the possible express parcel weighing 3 kg.
distractorReasons.C: STANDARD need not meet the express-only condition, while the EXPRESS record still needs a weight check.
distractorReasons.D: All four would include unnecessary checks; only EXPRESS and 3 kg can hide the forbidden combination.
